extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of classical Euclidean geometry; readers of Euclid Book III–IV
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted propositions, problems, definitions and corollaries from Euclid's Elements (Book III and start of Book IV) concerning circles, tangents, chords, arcs, and the inscription/circumscription of polygons and circles. Includes statements, constructions, and proof sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXVIII — Equal chords in equal circles cut off equal arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles, equal chords divide the circumferences into arcs which are equal each to each (lesser to lesser, greater to greater).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: Join centres to chord endpoints; equal radii give equal side pairs in two isosceles triangles, hence equal vertex angles at centres and equal subtended arcs. Notes: trivial when chords are diameters; deduce equality of remaining arcs by equality of whole circumferences. Exercises following give related locus/converse facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXIX — Equal arcs are subtended by equal chords
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles, equal arcs are subtended by equal chords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: Use equality of central angles for equal arcs; congruent isosceles triangles (equal radii and equal included angle) give equal bases (chords). Observation: because circles are equal they are congruent; statement holds by superposition. Useful converses to XXVIII.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXX — To bisect a given arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: Given arc ACB, construct its midpoint (point C that bisects arc AB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: Draw chord AB, bisect AB at D; erect DC ⟂ AB meeting the arc in C. Proof: Triangles ADC and BDC are congruent (AD = DB, DC common, right angles), so AC = BC and arcs are equal. Exercises: related chord/arc ratio problems and locus statements about bisectors and distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXI — Angles in semicircle/segments
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Angle in a semicircle is a right angle. (2) Angle in a segment greater than a semicircle is acute. (3) Angle in a segment less than a semicircle is obtuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: Use centre O and isosceles triangle symmetry to show angle at circumference equals adjacent angle formed with extension, hence right when diameter is base. Parts (2) and (3) follow by comparison with right angle. Corollaries: (1) diagonals of an inscribed parallelogram meet at the circle centre; (2) construction to find centre by carpenter's square; (3) draw two tangents from a point outside circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXII — Tangent-chord theorem (angle between tangent and chord)
rubrics_metrics.description: If EF is a tangent at A and chord AC is drawn, then the angle which the tangent makes with the chord equals the angle in the opposite (alternate) segment of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: If chord passes through centre, angles are right. Otherwise draw AB ⟂ tangent at A to locate centre; show sum of certain triangle angles equals right angle and deduce equality. Alternative proofs via cyclic quadrilaterals or method of limits. Lardner and Townsend references given. Exercises: many consequences about touching circles, parallel chords from common secants, and metric relations between tangents and chords.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXIII — To describe a circular segment on a given line containing a given angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: On given straight line AB, construct a circular segment that contains an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: If X is right, use semicircle. Otherwise construct angle BAE = X with AB, erect perpendiculars to locate diameter AC and construct circle on AC as diameter passing through B; angle in that segment equals X by previous tangent/chord relations. Exercises: loci and constructions for triangles given base & vertical angle and other constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXIV — To cut off from a circle a segment containing a given angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: From given circle ABC, cut off a segment whose inscribed angle equals given angle X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: Take A on circumference, draw tangent AD and mark point C so that angle DAC = X; chord AC cuts off desired segment. Proof by showing angle in alternate segment equals angle DAC.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXV — Intersecting chords theorem (product of segments)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at an interior point E, then AE·EB = CE·ED (the rectangles contained by the segments are equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: Multiple cases handled—(1) E is centre; (2) one chord passes through centre and meets other at right angles; (3) neither passes through centre; (4) general case by drawing diameter through intersection. Uses Pythagorean relations and right-triangle identities. Corollaries: relation between chord segments and radius; condition for four points to be concyclic; equiangular triangles give equal products of non-corresponding sides. Exercises and many further metric consequences follow (including Catalan's results about rectangles of chord pairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXV — Corollaries (product/difference identities and concyclicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several corollaries: (1) For chord cut at interior point, product of segments = radius^2 − (distance from centre to point)^2. (2) If products of segments of two intersecting lines are equal, their endpoints are concyclic. (3) In equiangular triangles, certain non-corresponding side-rectangles are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corollaries are immediate consequences of the main product theorem and are used throughout subsequent exercises (loci, construction problems, relations among arcs and chords).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Supplement of an arc
rubrics_metrics.description: The supplement of an arc is the difference between it and a semicircle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in subsequent propositions relating rectangles of chord lengths to chords of supplements and to radius; several exercises compute relations when sum/difference of arcs is less or greater than semicircle.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXV — Catalan-style chord-rectangle identities
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sum of two arcs AC, CB is less than a semicircle, the rectangle AC·CB (products of chord lengths) equals the rectangle of the radius and the excess of the chord of the supplement of their difference above the chord of the supplement of their sum; analogous identities when sums exceed a semicircle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration constructs diameters and parallel chords to relate supplements and employs previous results equating chord products to radius times certain chord differences or sums. These identities are presented with worked example and generalization; they are used for solving maximum/minimum and locus problems in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXVI — Tangent-secant theorem (external point)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a point P external to a circle two lines are drawn, one a tangent PT and one a secant through A and B (PA, PB), then AP·PB = (PT)^2 (the rectangle of the secant segments equals the square of the tangent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: consider cases where secant passes through centre or not; drop perpendiculars from centre; use Pythagorean relations and previous product relations for chords to derive equality. Extended statement: for a fixed external point P, the product AP·PB is constant for all chords through P. Corollaries: concyclicity condition for four points with equal products; equality of tangents from common chord points; concurrency of common chords of three intersecting circles. Exercises include a triangle-height/ratio problem using tangent-secant facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXVI — Corollaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Cor.1: If two lines AB, CD produced meet at P and AP·PB = CP·DP then A,B,C,D are concyclic. Cor.2: Tangents to two circles from any point in their common chord are equal. Cor.3: Common chords of any three intersecting circles are concurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are direct consequences of the tangent-secant product identity and used in constructions and locus arguments that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXVII — Converse tangent test
rubrics_metrics.description: If for a point P outside a circle the product AP·PB (for secant through A,B) equals the square on some line PT from P meeting the circle, then the line through the circle meeting it at the endpoint of that square (PT) is tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: Construct true tangent PQ, show PQ^2 equals given product, deduce PT = PQ, then isosceles triangle argument about equal sides from centre leads to right angle at PT so PT is tangent. Exercises: many construction problems (circles touching lines/circles, loci, tangent intersection angle problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: BOOK IV — Definitions i–iv (inscribed/circumscribed/regular)
rubrics_metrics.description: i. Inscribed/Described relationship between rectilineal figures. ii. A rectilineal figure inscribed in a circle when its vertices lie on circumference; conversely circle circumscribed about figure. iii. A circle inscribed in a rectilineal figure when it touches each side; conversely input circumscribed about. iv. A rectilineal figure equilateral and equiangular is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These basic definitions set terminology for Book IV constructions and problems about inscribing and describing polygons and circles. Observation summarizes structure of Book IV (triangles, squares, pentagons, miscellaneous — all problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IV. I — Place chord equal to given straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: In a given circle ABC, place a chord equal to a given straight line D not greater than the diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take diameter AC; cut off AE = D from AC; with center A and radius AE draw circle that meets original circle at B (and F); AB is required chord. Proof: AB = AE = D. Elementary tool for mapping given lengths into chord lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IV. II — Inscribe triangle equiangular to given triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: In given circle ABC, inscribe triangle equiangular to given triangle DEF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: at chosen point A draw tangent GH; make angles at A equal to E and F respectively; join B and C on circumference to form triangle ABC equiangular to DEF. Proof: Use tangent-chord theorem to equate constructed angles to corresponding interior angles of the inscribed triangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IV. III — Describe triangle about a given circle equiangular to given triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: About given circle ABC, construct triangle equiangular to given triangle DEF (i.e., circumscribe a triangle with given angle measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: extend a side of DEF, choose radius points A,B,C on circle, make central angles equal to corresponding exterior angles of triangle; draw tangents at A,B,C to form triangle LMN. Proof: angle relations via right angles at tangent points and equality of central angles produce equal corresponding angles in LMN and DEF.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IV. IV — Inscribe a circle in a given triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: To inscribe a circle in triangle ABC (construct incircle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect two angles (AO, BO); their intersection O is incenter; drop perpendiculars to sides to find contact points; circle with centre O and radius to contact point is incircle. Proof: equal perpendicular distances from centre to sides; standard properties of angle bisectors. Exercises: relations of contact distances (s−a etc.), escribed circles and many metric area relations (rs = area, Heron formula derivations given).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IV. V — Describe a circle about a given triangle (circumcircle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: Construct the circumcircle of triangle ABC (circle through all three vertices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect two sides BC, AC at D and E; erect perpendiculars DO and EO to those sides; their intersection O is circumcentre; circle with centre O through A,B,C is circumcircle. Proof: congruent right-triangle arguments show OA=OB=OC. Corollary: perpendicular bisectors of sides are concurrent. Definition: circle is circumcircle, its radius circumradius, centre circumcentre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises and examination questions (Book III & IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list of exercises and examination-style questions following the propositions, covering constructions, loci, maximum/minimum problems, metric relations (sums/differences of chords and squares), concurrency, concyclicity tests, relations of tangents, and many classical Euclidean problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises test application of the preceding propositions (angles in segments, tangent-chord theorem, intersecting chord products, tangent-secant identities, circle inscription/circumscription constructions). Specific problems include: locus of centres touching circle at given point, constructing circles tangent to lines/circles, various optimization locus problems, and many triangle-circle relations (e.g., distances from vertices to contact points, relations yielding Heron's formula). They serve as practice and extension rather than new theorems.
